status_reasoning: Reviewers acknowledge the vesicle clustering data but express concern that 'the concentration of synuclein used in the experiments is very high (2–20 μM), resulting in high protein:lipid ratios, raising the possibility that the liposomes are completely covered with protein.' They request experiments to test whether such high concentrations are required, questioning the physiological relevance of the observed clustering.

Reviewers question the mechanistic interpretation, asking 'whether vesicle aggregation is caused by homooligomerization of synuclein between membranes.' While the data show clustering depends on binding to both lipids and synaptobrevin-2, reviewers request additional experiments to clarify the mechanism, indicating uncertainty about the proposed dual-binding model.

All referees explicitly rejected the proposed model, stating it 'seems highly speculative and almost counter-intuitive' because 'the data presented in the paper actually show a reduction of docking between v-vesicles and t-vesicles by addition of α-synuclein.' Reviewers challenge the model by asking 'wouldn't one expect a substantial effect of synuclein KO on neurotransmitter release?' and cite contradictory findings from Choi et al. (2013).

Reviewers do not question the fusion data showing that α-synuclein has little effect on Ca2+-triggered fusion. This finding is implicitly accepted as it forms part of the basis for their critique of the model, and no concerns are raised about these specific experimental observations.

The A30P mutant data showing impaired lipid binding and reduced clustering is not questioned by reviewers. These findings support the lipid-binding requirement for clustering and are accepted without critique.
